claim: Reduced levels of CVB3, poliovirus, and enterovirus D68 infection were observed in WASL KO cells.

claim: Wiskostatin is a small molecule inhibitor of WASL.

claim: By a multi-step growth analysis, NCK1 KO showed 10-fold reduction of EMCV virus titer at 24 hr post infection.

claim: NCK1 KO showed 14-fold reduction of CVB3 titer at 36 hr post infection.
source: By a multi-step growth analysis, NCK1 KO showed 10-fold reduction of EMCV virus titer at 24 hr post infection (P<0.01 Figure 2I) and 14-fold reduction of CVB3 titer at 36 hr post infection (p<0.05, Figure 2K).

claim: Ectopic expression of NCK1 in the NCK1 KO cells rescued EMCV infection to wild type levels.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C D.

claim: EMCV infection levels and viral titer production in the double and triple knockout lines were the same as observed in the TNK2 KO1 lines.

claim: The lack of an additive effect in double and triple knockouts suggests that WASL and NCK1 are both in the same genetic pathway as TNK2.

claim: TNK2 can phosphorylate WASL.

source: Combined with the known ability of TNK2 to phosphorylate WASL (Yokoyama et al., 2005), these data support a model where TNK2 acts upstream of WASL and NCK1.

claim: The magnitude of the impact of TNK2 KO1 was greater than that of WASL KO or NCK1 KO.

source: The magnitude of the impact of TNK2 KO1 was greater than that of WASL KO or NCK1 KO, suggesting that TNK2 might work through additional pathways in mediating virus infection besides acting through WASL and NCK1.

claim: TNK2 phosphorylation of WASL increases its actin nucleation activity.
source: Because TNK2 phosphorylation of WASL increases its actin nucleation activity (Yokoyama and Miller, 2003), we reasoned that it might be possible to complement the TNK2 deficiency by overexpression of WASL.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yokoyama and Miller, 2003.

claim: Overexpression of wild type WASL in the TNK2 KO1 A549 cells led to increased EMCV virus infection.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Constitutively active point mutants of WASL have been described.
source: Since constitutively active point mutants of WASL have been described (Adamovich et al., 2009; Keszei et al., 2018) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B C), we next tested whether overexpression of three such constructs in the TNK2 KO1 cells could further increase virus infection.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Adamovich et al., 2009; Keszei et al., 2018.

claim: A higher level of complementation for all three constitutively active WASL mutants was observed compared to wild type WASL in TNK2 KO1 cells.
source: A higher level of complementation for all three mutants was observed compared to wild type WASL (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Constitutively active WASL fully rescued the NCK1 KO virus infection phenotype.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplements 2D, 3C.

claim: TNK2, WASL, and NCK1 are in a pathway to support picornavirus infection with WASL and NCK1 downstream of TNK2.
source: Together, these data demonstrated that TNK2, WASL, and NCK1 are in a pathway to support picornavirus infection with WASL and NCK1 downstream of TNK2.
evidence: This is an inference based on genetic epistasis analysis and complementation experiments.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to Donnelly et al., 2013.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to Galisteo et al., 2006.

claim: WASL and NCK1 both distributed homogenously throughout the cytoplasm when individually expressed in 293T cells.
source: Fluorescent protein tagged forms of TNK2, WASL, and NCK1 were individually expressed in 293 T cells. evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TNK2 formed puncta in the cytoplasm when individually expressed in 293T cells.
source: Fluorescent protein tagged forms of TNK2, WASL, and NCK1 were individually expressed in 293 T cells. evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citations to Teo et al., 2001; Shen et al., 2011.

claim: Co-expression of mCerulean tagged TNK2 with mVenus tagged NCK1 re-localized NCK1 into the puncta observed by TNK2 expression alone.
source: Co-expression of mCerulean tagged TNK2 with mVenus tagged NCK1 re-localized NCK1 into the puncta observed by TNK2 expression alone (Figure 3—figure supplements 1, 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1, 4A.

claim: Co-expression of mCerulean tagged WASL with mVenus tagged NCK1 showed homogenous distribution in the cytoplasm and co-localization of these two proteins.
source: Co-expression of mCerulean tagged WASL with mVenus tagged NCK1 showed homogenous distribution in the cytoplasm and co-localization of these two proteins (Figure 3—figure supplements 1, 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1, 4A.

claim: WASL and NCK1 had higher FRET efficiency in cells.
source: Further analysis by quantitative FRET demonstrated that WASL and NCK1 had higher FRET efficiency in cells, while TNK2 and NCK1 also had significant, but lower, FRET efficiency (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A B.

claim: TNK2 and NCK1 had significant, but lower, FRET efficiency in cells.
source: Further analysis by quantitative FRET demonstrated that WASL and NCK1 had higher FRET efficiency in cells, while TNK2 and NCK1 also had significant, but lower, FRET efficiency (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A B.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of FLAG tagged NCK1 pulled down HA tagged WASL more efficiently than it did Myc tagged TNK2.
source: Consistent with the FRET data, in co-transfected 293 T cells, immunoprecipitation of FLAG tagged NCK1 pulled down HA tagged WASL more efficiently than it did Myc tagged TNK2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4C.

claim: TNK2 and WASL bind directly to NCK1.
source: Altogether, these data demonstrate that TNK2 and WASL bind directly to NCK1.
evidence: This is an inference based on FRET and immunoprecipitation data.

claim: The TNK2 KO1, WASL KO, and NCK1 KO cells produced the same titers of EMCV virus as the control cells at 10 hr post transfection of EMCV genomic RNA.
source: To begin dissecting the stage of the EMCV virus lifecycle impacted by TNK2, WASL, and NCK1, we transfected EMCV genomic RNA into the cells to bypass the early stages of the viral lifecycle. The TNK2 KO1, WASL KO, and NCK1 KO cells produced the same titers of EMCV virus as the control cells at 10 hr post transfection (Figure 4A) demonstrating that TNK2, WASL, and NCK1 are dispensable for EMCV replication and post-replication stages of the EMCV lifecycle.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: TNK2, WASL, and NCK1 are dispensable for EMCV replication and post-replication stages of the EMCV lifecycle.
source: To begin dissecting the stage of the EMCV virus lifecycle impacted by TNK2, WASL, and NCK1, we transfected EMCV genomic RNA into the cells to bypass the early stages of the viral lifecycle. The TNK2 KO1, WASL KO, and NCK1 KO cells produced the same titers of EMCV virus as the control cells at 10 hr post transfection (Figure 4A) demonstrating that TNK2, WASL, and NCK1 are dispensable for EMCV replication and post-replication stages of the EMCV lifecycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA transfection experiment shown in Figure 4A.

claim: All three genes (TNK2, WASL, and NCK1) act on an early stage of the viral lifecycle.
source: Thus, we concluded that all three genes act on an early stage of the viral lifecycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA transfection experiment.

claim: Aim-100 pre-treatment reduced EMCV infection, but administration after virus inoculation had no effect.
source: As a second line of evidence, we determined the impact of adding the TNK2 kinase-specific inhibitor Aim-100 before or at varying times after EMCV infection. While Aim-100 pre-treatment reduced EMCV infection, administration after virus inoculation had no effect (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), consistent with a role for TNK2 at an early stage of virus infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: No difference in virus binding was observed among control, TNK2 KO1, and WASL KO cells.
source: We examined the impact of TNK2 and WASL deletion on virus binding, virus internalization, pore formation, and viral RNA genome translocation. Following incubation at 4°C for one hour, no difference in virus binding was observed among control, TNK2 KO1, and WASL KO cells (Figure 4C), as assessed by qRT-PCR for EMCV genomic RNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There was a 46% reduction of intracellular EMCV viral RNA in the TNK2 KO1 cells after internalization.
source: In contrast, after raising the temperature to 37° C for 30 min to allow for internalization of the bound virus particles and then trypsinization to remove uninternalized surface virus particles as described before (Berry and Tse, 2017; Hackett et al., 2015), there was a 46% reduction (p<0.001) of intracellular EMCV viral RNA in the TNK2 KO1 cells (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–E.

claim: No difference in RNA levels was observed in WASL KO cells after internalization.
source: However, no difference in RNA levels was observed in WASL KO cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: 25% fewer EMCV positive TNK2 KO1 cells were observed compared to control cells using fluorescently labeled EMCV virions.
source: As a complementary approach, we evaluated internalization using fluorescently labeled EMCV virions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A B). 25% fewer EMCV positive TNK2 KO1 cells were observed compared to control cells (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), while no statistical difference was observed in the WASL KO cells (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: No statistical difference in internalization of fluorescently labeled EMCV was observed in the WASL KO cells.
source: As a complementary approach, we evaluated internalization using fluorescently labeled EMCV virions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A B). 25% fewer EMCV positive TNK2 KO1 cells were observed compared to control cells (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), while no statistical difference was observed in the WASL KO cells (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Transferrin was internalized in TNK2 KO1 and WASL KO cells to the same level as in the control cells.
source: We examined the ability of fluorescently labeled transferrin, a known cargo for clathrin-mediated endocytosis, to be endocytosed in both TNK2 KO1 and WASL KO cells. Transferrin was internalized in TNK2 KO1 and WASL KO cells to the same level as in the control cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A B), consistent with a previous report that knock down of TNK2 has no effect on transferrin endocytosis (Grøvdal et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A B and a citation to Grøvdal et al., 2008.

claim: No defect in uptake of Dextran was observed in TNK2 KO1 cells.
source: To further check other general virus entry pathways, we also examined whether macropinocytosis was affected in these cells. FITC conjugated Dextran (7 KDa) is reported to be uptaken by macropinocytosis (Oppliger et al., 2016). No defect in uptake of Dextran was observed in TNK2 KO1 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C D.

claim: The WASL KO cells had a 75% reduction in Dextran uptake.
source: In contrast, the WASL KO cells had a 75% reduction in Dextran uptake (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C D), which is consistent with the known dependency of macropinocytosis on actin polymerization (Innocenti et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C D and a citation to Innocenti et al., 2005.

claim: TNK2 KO1 and WASL KO cells showed no defect in virus pore formation during EMCV infection.
source: A step that is closely linked to internalization for picornaviruses is virus-induced pore formation, which is required for genome release into the cytoplasm. To assess pore formation, cells were treated with the membrane impermeable translation inhibitor, α-sarcin. Virus-induced pore formation will lead to translation inhibition and reduction of 35S methionine and 35S cysteine incorporation whereas in the absence of pore formation, translation will proceed at wild type levels (Fernández-Puentes and Carrasco, 1980). TNK2 KO1 and WASL KO cells showed no defect in virus pore formation during EMCV infection (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: eIF4G cleavage in presence or absence of a virus genome replication inhibitor guanidine hydrochloride showed no difference in the WASL KO cells as compared to the control cells.
source: To determine whether TNK2 or WASL plays any role in downstream viral RNA genome translocation after pore formation, we examined virus-induced host protein cleavage after its entry. For some picornaviruses, immediately after translocation of its genome, translation of the incoming positive strand RNA leads to proteolytic cleavage of the host protein eIF4G to shut down host translation (Glaser and Skern, 2000). Since this activity has not been described for EMCV, we used CVB3 which is known to have this activity (Carthy et al., 1998). eIF4G cleavage in presence or absence of a virus genome replication inhibitor guanidine hydrochloride showed no difference in the WASL KO cells as compared to the control cells, demonstrating that WASL does not impact this step of the viral lifecycle.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: WASL does not impact eIF4G cleavage step of the viral lifecycle.
source: eIF4G cleavage in presence or absence of a virus genome replication inhibitor guanidine hydrochloride showed no difference in the WASL KO cells as compared to the control cells, demonstrating that WASL does not impact this step of the viral lifecycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the eIF4G cleavage experiment shown in Figure 4G.

claim: A decrease of eIF4G cleavage was observed in TNK2 KO1 cells.
source: In contrast, we observed a decrease of eIF4G cleavage in TNK2 KO1 cells, suggesting that TNK2 might play a role in this process.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: TNK2 is present in endocytic vesicles and colocalizes with the early endosome marker EEA1.
source: TNK2 is present in endocytic vesicles and colocalizes with the early endosome marker EEA1 (Teo et al., 2001; Shen et al., 2011; Grøvdal et al., 2008; Jones et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Teo et al., 2001; Shen et al., 2011; Grøvdal et al., 2008; Jones et al., 2014.

claim: High TNK2 expression formed GFP aggregates inside the cytosol of cells in about 80% of the cell population.
source: To visualize TNK2 subcellular localization, we expressed N-terminally GFP tagged TNK2 in the TNK2 KO1 cells. evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B and C and citations to Teo et al., 2001; Prieto-Echagüe et al., 2010.

claim: Low TNK2 expression was observed inside the cytosol of cells in about 20% of the cell population.
source: To visualize TNK2 subcellular localization, we expressed N-terminally GFP tagged TNK2 in the TNK2 KO1 cells. Two different patterns were observed in GFP positive cells: high TNK2 expression formed GFP aggregates inside the cytosol of cells in about 80% of the cell population, which has been described previously (Teo et al., 2001; Prieto-Echagüe et al., 2010), and low TNK2 expression inside the cytosol of cells in about 20% of the cell population (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B and C.

claim: N-terminally GFP tagged TNK2 expression in the TNK2 KO1 cells statistically increased virus infection from 17.2% to 22.0% of GFP-transduced control cell infection.
source: Consistent with the native TNK2 rescue, N-terminally GFP tagged TNK2 expression in the TNK2 KO1 cells statistically increased virus infection from 17.2% to 22.0% of GFP-transduced control cell infection (p<0.01, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In TNK2 KO1 cells with high TNK2 expression that formed aggregates, no GFP-TNK2 in proximity to EMCV was observed.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In cells with low TNK2 expression, labeled EMCV particles were observed in proximity to GFP-TNK2.
source: However, in cells with low TNK2 expression, labeled EMCV particles were observed in proximity to GFP-TNK2 (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), presumably in early endosomes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: About 40% of the EMCV particles were in proximity to GFP-TNK2 in cells with low TNK2 expression.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dodding and Way, 2009.

claim: Both TNK2 and WASL are activated by the upstream CDC42 small GTPase.
source: Both TNK2 and WASL are activated by the upstream CDC42 small GTPase (Galisteo et al., 2006; Grøvdal et al., 2008; Howlin et al., 2008; Mahajan et al., 2007; Rohatgi et al., 2000), which can be inhibited by pirl1 (Oppliger et al., 2016).

source: Both TNK2 and WASL are activated by the upstream CDC42 small GTPase (Galisteo et al., 2006; Grøvdal et al., 2008; Howlin et al., 2008; Mahajan et al., 2007; Rohatgi et al., 2000), which can be inhibited by pirl1 (Oppliger et al., 2016).
